name: Ksheera Ramalingeswara Swamy Temple, Palakollu
deity: Shiva as Ksheera Ramalingeswara, with his consort Parvati
period: Eastern Chalukya (9th century, King Bhima); additions completed by the 14th century
summary: At Palakollu stands Ksheerarama, its milk-white linga naming the temple beneath a nine-storey gopuram near 120 feet — among the tallest of the five Pancharama shrines, where a day of worship is said to equal a year at Kashi.

sections.history: Ksheerarama is one of the five Pancharama Kshetras, the ancient Shiva temples strung across the deltaic country of coastal Andhra Pradesh. The town of Palakollu grew up in West Godavari district near the great river and close to Narasapuram, and the temple has stood at its heart through many centuries of worship. The sanctum is credited to the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in the ninth century, under a king remembered as Bhima, the dynasty most closely associated with the Pancharama group. What the visitor sees today, however, is the work of many hands over many generations: the towering gopuram and the wider complex were built up and completed only by the fourteenth century, as later medieval patrons enlarged and embellished the shrine. That long, layered making — Chalukyan foundations carried forward and elaborated — is written into the temple's Dravidian architecture, and it has remained a living centre of Shaiva devotion ever since.
sections.architecture: The presiding linga of Ksheerarama is milky-white — ksheera means milk — and it is one of the taller lingas of the Pancharama circuit, a pale column that gives the shrine both its name and its distinctive character. Rising over the complex is the temple's most famous feature: a gopuram close to 120 feet high, climbing through nine diminishing storeys, counted among the tallest of the five temples and visible far across the flat delta country. Before the sanctum stretches a great mandapa carried on seventy-two pillars of black stone, their dark shafts a deliberate foil to the white linga within. Subsidiary shrines to Gokarneswara, Ganesha, Kartikeya and Vishnu ring the enclosure, a central Nandi keeps its watch toward the god, and a broad temple tank completes the sacred ground, mirroring the great tower in still water.
sections.legends: Ksheerarama belongs to the shared origin story of the Pancharama Kshetras: the linga once worn by the asura Tarakasura, which made him invincible, was shattered by Kartikeya's fire-weapon at Vishnu's counsel and fell in five pieces, each fixed where it landed and enshrined. Here devotional memory adds two threads of its own. The linga is said to have been installed and worshipped by Vishnu himself, and tradition links the temple with Rama, remembered as having worshipped a linga at this spot — hence the name Rama-lingeswara, though the Rama link is cherished lore rather than documented history. A much-loved saying holds that a single day of worship here carries the merit of a full year at Kashi, the holy city of Varanasi.
sections.festivals: The temple's great annual occasion is Maha Shivaratri, the night sacred to Shiva, when devotees keep vigil through the dark hours and the shrine draws its largest gatherings of the year. The other principal celebration is the Kalyanotsavam, the ceremonial marriage of Ksheera Ramalingeswara and Parvati, enacted with music, ritual and festal splendour. Around these peaks Shaiva worship keeps its steady rhythm year-round; during the great festivals the temple's hours lengthen well beyond the usual.
sections.experience: To arrive at Ksheerarama is first to see its tower — the nine-storey gopuram lifts above Palakollu and the surrounding delta, guiding pilgrims in from a distance. Stepping through it, you pass into the hall of seventy-two black pillars, cool and shadowed, before reaching the pale milk-white linga at its heart. Move slowly around the enclosure to greet the smaller shrines of Gokarneswara, Ganesha, Kartikeya and Vishnu, pause before the central Nandi, and walk out to the temple tank where the great gopuram lies reflected. Mornings and evenings, when lamps are lit and the delta light is soft, hold the quiet devotional mood best.

visit.timings: Generally open daily from about 6 am to 12 noon and again from 4 pm to 8 pm; timings extend during Maha Shivaratri, Kalyanotsavam and other festivals, when the temple stays open well into the night.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — covered shoulders and legs in keeping with a living place of worship; footwear is removed and left outside before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas and around the great gopuram and tank, but not inside the inner sanctum before the linga; look for posted notices and follow the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Palakollu has its own railway station within the town, making arrival by train straightforward; the nearest airports are Rajahmundry (RJA) and Vijayawada (VGA), each a road journey away, and Palakollu is well connected by road, close to Narasapuram in West Godavari district.
